32093: A quiet link in a long chain, known only by his family.
32099: Aaron marries Elisheba, Amminadab's daughter and Nahshon's sister. So the priestly line of Aaron and the royal line of Judah are joined by marriage.
32101: His son Nahshon becomes the leader of Judah in the wilderness.
32102: Amminadab is Ram's son and Nahshon's father, in the line from Judah to David. He matters for another reason too: his daughter Elisheba married Aaron, so the mother of Israel's priests came from the family of Israel's future kings.
32103: Father of Nahshon and of Elisheba, Aaron's wife. Listed in the genealogies of Ruth, Chronicles, Matthew and Luke.
32104: A respected elder of Judah who married his daughter into the priesthood.
32109: leader of the tribe of Judah
32112: He is named head of Judah for the census and camps at the front, on the east side of the tabernacle.
32114: When the tabernacle is dedicated, Nahshon brings the first of the twelve tribal offerings.
32116: When Israel sets out from Sinai, Judah's division under Nahshon goes first.
32117: Nahshon son of Amminadab was the chief of Judah during the wilderness years. He led the first tribe in the camp and on the march, and brought the first offering at the tabernacle's dedication. His sister Elisheba was Aaron's wife. He stands in David's family line and in Jesus' genealogy.
32118: Son of Amminadab, brother-in-law of Aaron, leader of Judah at Sinai. He brought the first dedication offering and led the march. Father of Salmon.
32119: At the Red Sea, when the tribes hesitated, Nahshon was the first to walk into the water, and the sea parted only after it reached his neck.
32121: Decisive and dutiful, the kind of leader who steps out first.
32127: Matthew records that Salmon fathered Boaz by Rahab, the woman of Jericho who hid Israel's spies.
32128: Nahshon fathers Salmon, and Salmon fathers Boaz.
32129: Salmon is Nahshon's son and Boaz's father. Only Matthew tells us his wife was Rahab, the Canaanite from Jericho who sheltered the spies. That means Boaz, who later married Ruth the Moabite, had a foreign mother himself. Matthew includes these women to show outsiders welcomed into Israel's royal line.
32130: Son of Nahshon, husband of Rahab, father of Boaz. Chronicles spells his name Salma.
32132: Only four generations (Salmon, Boaz, Obed, Jesse) span roughly 300 years from the conquest to David. Most scholars, conservative and critical, think the genealogy skips generations, as ancient genealogies often did. Others suggest very long lives.
32133: Rabbinic tradition says Rahab married Joshua, not Salmon. Matthew's account differs from this.
32135: Some suggest Salmon was one of the two spies Rahab hid, but the Bible does not say so.
32136: A man of Judah who married across a line others would not cross.
32142: The king of Egypt commands Shiphrah and Puah to kill every Hebrew boy at birth.
32144: Because they fear God, they let the boys live. When the king demands why, they say the Hebrew women give birth before a midwife arrives.
32146: God deals well with the midwives and gives them families of their own.
32147: Shiphrah and Puah were midwives who refused Pharaoh's order to kill newborn Hebrew boys. Their story is the first recorded act of civil disobedience in the Bible: they 'feared God' more than the king. Strikingly, Exodus names these two midwives but never names the Pharaoh. Their answer to the king was clever, and perhaps not fully true, but God blessed them.
32148: One of two midwives commanded to kill Hebrew boys. She feared God and saved them, gave the king an explanation about Hebrew women giving birth quickly, and God gave her a household.
32150: Some say God rewarded their fear of him, not their deception. Others argue that misleading a murderous ruler is right when lives are at stake. Christians have cited them in debates about lying to protect the innocent.
32152: The Hebrew can mean 'Hebrew midwives' or 'midwives to the Hebrews'. Josephus thought they were Egyptian. Their names are Semitic, which suggests Hebrews.
32153: Shiphrah and Puah were Jochebed (Moses' mother) and Miriam under other names.
32154: Calm, quick-witted and unafraid of kings, because she fears God more.
32158: With Shiphrah she disobeys the king's command to kill Hebrew boys at birth and explains herself cleverly when summoned.
32160: Because the midwives feared God, he made them houses (families).
32161: Puah was the second of the two midwives who defied Pharaoh's order to kill Hebrew baby boys. Her courage, with Shiphrah's, kept the boys of Israel alive in the generation of Moses. She should not be confused with Puah of Issachar (Judges 10:1), a man with a similar name.
32162: One of two midwives who feared God, disobeyed the king, and were rewarded with households of their own.
32163: Puah was Miriam, called Puah because she cooed to the newborns.
32164: Gentle with babies and firm with tyrants.
32174: Cutting and setting stones; wood carving
32175: Filled with the Spirit of God for craftsmanship
32178: God tells Moses he has called Bezalel by name and filled him with the Spirit of God, with wisdom, understanding and knowledge in every craft.
32180: Oholiab of Dan is appointed to work with him, and other skilled workers are given wisdom.
32182: Moses announces Bezalel's calling to the people and says God has put it in his heart to teach others.
32184: With the workers he makes the tabernacle, and personally makes the ark of the covenant with its gold cover and cherubim.
32186: Centuries later Solomon worships at the bronze altar 'that Bezaleel had made'.
32187: Bezalel son of Uri, grandson of Hur, from the tribe of Judah, was the master craftsman who built the tabernacle and the ark of the covenant. He is the first person named in the Bible as 'filled with the Spirit of God', and the gift was for art and craftsmanship: gold, stone, wood and design. God also gave him the ability to teach others. His story shows that skilled manual work and beauty can be a calling from God, not just preaching or leadership.
32188: Son of Uri son of Hur, of Judah. Called by name and filled with God's Spirit for every kind of craft. Worked with Oholiab and led the craftsmen who built the tabernacle and its furniture, including the ark.
32189: Bezalel is the classic biblical example of the Spirit equipping artists and workers, often cited in discussions of faith and work.
32190: The rabbis said Bezalel 'knew how to combine the letters by which heaven and earth were created', linking his building of the tabernacle to God's creation of the world (b. Berakhot 55a).
32191: Scholars note many echoes between the building of the tabernacle and the creation account in Genesis 1, making Bezalel's work a small copy of God's.
32192: Absorbed, careful and joyful in his work, speaking of materials and measurements with reverence.
32194: uncertain; possibly 'white linen' or from the Egyptian god Horus
32198: During the battle with Amalek, Aaron and Hur hold up Moses' tired hands, one on each side, until sunset, and Israel wins.
32200: When Moses goes up the mountain he tells the elders that Aaron and Hur are with them to settle disputes.
32201: Hur was a leader who, with Aaron, held up Moses' arms during the battle against Amalek at Rephidim. Moses later left him with Aaron in charge of the people. The craftsman Bezalel is called 'son of Uri, son of Hur', and 1 Chronicles traces this Hur back to Judah through Hezron and Caleb. Most readers assume this is the same Hur, though the text never says so directly. Hur then drops out of the story, and he is not mentioned in the golden calf episode.
32202: With Aaron he held up Moses' hands at Rephidim, and he was left with Aaron to judge cases while Moses was on Sinai. A Hur of Judah was the grandfather of Bezalel.
32203: Hur is a model for supporters who hold up leaders in prayer and practical help.
32204: Some midrash says Hur was killed for resisting the making of the golden calf, which is why he disappears from the story. This is not in the text.
32205: Hur was the husband of Miriam, Moses' sister.
32207: Loyal and steady, more comfortable supporting than leading.
32213: With Moses, Aaron, Abihu and seventy elders he goes up the mountain, sees the God of Israel, and eats and drinks in his presence.
32215: He is set apart with his father and brothers to serve as priest.
32217: On the day the priesthood begins, Nadab and Abihu offer 'strange fire' which God had not commanded. Fire comes from the LORD and kills them.
32218: Nadab was Aaron's eldest son and was ordained as a priest. He was one of the few who went up Mount Sinai and saw God. Yet on the first day of his priestly service he and his brother Abihu offered 'strange fire', incense or fire God had not commanded, and fire from the LORD killed them. Moses explained it with God's words: 'I will be sanctified in them that come nigh me.' He died without children.
32219: Eldest son of Aaron and Elisheba. Saw God on Sinai, was ordained priest, offered unauthorised fire with Abihu, and died before the LORD with no sons.
32221: Rabbis suggested several faults: they were drunk (the ban on priests drinking follows in Leviticus 10:9), they acted without consulting Moses, or they were impatient to take over leadership.
32222: The story teaches that worship must be on God's terms, and that closeness to God brings greater responsibility.
32223: What made the fire 'strange' is unclear: wrong source of coals, wrong time, wrong incense or wrong place. The text focuses on the fact that God had not commanded it.
32224: Eager and privileged, perhaps too sure of his own access to God.
32228: He is among those who see God on Sinai and eat and drink before him.
32229: With Nadab he offers unauthorised fire before the LORD and is struck dead.
32231: Their cousins carry the bodies out. Aaron 'held his peace', and he and his remaining sons are told not to show public mourning while on duty.
32232: Abihu was Aaron's second son and a priest. With his older brother Nadab he saw God on Mount Sinai, and with Nadab he died on the first day of priestly service after offering fire God had not commanded. Their deaths left Eleazar and Ithamar to carry on Aaron's line. The story stands as a stark warning that being near God is serious.
32233: Second son of Aaron. Saw God at Sinai, was ordained priest, offered unauthorised fire with Nadab, and died childless before the LORD.
32234: Interpreters read his death alongside Nadab's; see Nadab for the main views on what went wrong.
32235: Close to his brother in everything, bold in worship but careless of the boundaries.
32241: He supervises the Levites' record of materials used to build the tabernacle.
32243: After his brothers' deaths, Moses is angry that Eleazar and Ithamar burned a sin offering instead of eating it. Aaron answers for them, and Moses accepts his reasoning.
32245: He directs the Levite clans that carry the tabernacle's curtains, frames and posts.
32247: In David's time the priests are divided into twenty-four groups: sixteen from Eleazar's line and eight from Ithamar's.
32248: Ithamar was Aaron's youngest son. After his older brothers Nadab and Abihu died, he and Eleazar carried on the priesthood. He was a capable administrator who kept the tabernacle accounts and supervised the Levites who carried it. His descendants formed one of the two priestly houses. Many interpreters believe Eli the priest of Shiloh came from his line.
32249: Youngest son of Aaron. Ordained as priest, supervised the tabernacle records and two Levite clans, and founded one of the two branches of the priesthood (with Eleazar's).
32251: Eli's family descended from Ithamar, since Ahimelech and Abiathar (Eli's descendants) are counted among Ithamar's sons in 1 Chronicles 24:3. Josephus says the same. The Bible never states it in one place, so the link is an inference.
32252: Careful, orderly and humble, a man who keeps the lists straight.
32256: Takes from the devoted things at Jericho
32257: Joshua warns that everything in Jericho is 'devoted' to the LORD: to be destroyed, or given to the LORD's treasury. Achan secretly takes some of it.
32259: A small Israelite force is routed at Ai and thirty-six men die. The people's courage melts.
32261: God tells Joshua that Israel has sinned. By casting lots, tribe by tribe and family by family, Achan is identified.
32263: Achan admits he saw a fine robe from Babylonia, 200 shekels of silver and a gold bar, 'coveted them, and took them', and buried them under his tent.
32264: Stoned in the Valley of Achor
32265: The goods are found. Achan, his family, animals and possessions are taken to the Valley of Achor ('trouble'), stoned and burned, and a heap of stones is raised over them.
32266: Achan, from the tribe of Judah, secretly kept valuable plunder from Jericho that God had commanded to be devoted to him. Because of this, Israel lost its next battle at Ai. When he was identified by lot he confessed, and he and his household were executed in the Valley of Achor ('Valley of Trouble'). His story teaches that one person's hidden sin can harm the whole community. It is also one of the Bible's hardest passages, because his family died with him. Later the prophet Hosea promised that the Valley of Achor would become 'a door of hope'.
32267: Son of Carmi, of Judah's clan of Zerah. He took a Babylonian robe, silver and gold from Jericho and hid them. Israel was defeated at Ai. He was found by lot, confessed, and was stoned with his family and possessions in the Valley of Achor. The story is recalled in Joshua 22:20 and 1 Chronicles 2:7.
32269: Israel is treated as one body: 'Israel hath sinned' (Joshua 7:11). The story shows how seriously God takes the holiness of the community at a founding moment, a theme later seen with Ananias and Sapphira (Acts 5).
32271: Some think the family knew about the goods buried under the tent and shared the guilt. Others note that Deuteronomy 24:16 forbids punishing children for parents' sins and see this as a unique 'devoted thing' case, where contact made the whole household devoted. Still others find the passage morally troubling and read it as reflecting ancient views of collective guilt.
32272: His confession follows a pattern often preached on: I saw, I coveted, I took, I hid, echoing the sin in Eden (Genesis 3:6).
32274: Greed and concealment that cost thirty-six lives
32277: Defensive at first, then broken and frank: 'I saw, I coveted, I took.'
32284: Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah and Tirzah
32287: Courage to bring a just case before Moses and God
32289: Their father Zelophehad has died with no sons. They stand before Moses, Eleazar and the leaders at the tabernacle and ask: why should our father's name vanish because he had no son? Give us land among his brothers.
32291: Moses brings their case before the LORD, who answers, 'The daughters of Zelophehad speak right.' A new law follows: if a man has no son, his inheritance passes to his daughter.
32293: Leaders of their clan worry that the land will pass to another tribe if the daughters marry outside. Moses rules they may marry whom they wish within their father's tribe. They marry their cousins.
32295: In Canaan they remind Eleazar and Joshua of Moses' ruling and receive their inheritance among the men of Manasseh.
32296: Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah and Tirzah were five sisters from the tribe of Manasseh. Their father died in the wilderness without sons, so under the usual custom his land would go to other men of the family. The sisters asked Moses publicly to give them their father's share. Moses took their case to God, who said they were right, and a new inheritance law was made for daughters. They followed up years later and received their land in Canaan. Their story is often cited as an example of women seeking justice within God's law, and of law developing to meet new cases.
32297: Five daughters of Zelophehad son of Hepher, of Manasseh. They petitioned Moses, God approved their claim, and the law of inheritance was extended to daughters. They were asked to marry within their tribe, did so, and received land west of the Jordan.
32298: The rabbis praised them as wise, interpreters of the law, and righteous, and noted they waited for the right moment to speak (b. Bava Batra 119b).
32300: They are often held up as models of faith-filled advocacy. Some stress that their goal was to preserve their father's name and land, not to overturn the family system; others stress that God sided with women's claims against custom.
32301: The two chapters (Numbers 27 and 36) show how ancient Israelite law was expected to grow through real cases and divine rulings.
32302: Respectful but unafraid, speaking together with one clear argument.
32308: Og comes out with his army to fight Israel at Edrei. God tells Moses not to fear, and Israel defeats Og and takes his sixty fortified cities.
32310: Og was the last of the Rephaim (a race of giants). His iron bed (or basalt coffin), nine cubits long, about four metres, was kept at Rabbah in Ammon.
32312: Psalms celebrate God's victory over Sihon and Og as part of how he gave Israel the land.
32313: Og was the Amorite king of Bashan, the fertile land east of the Sea of Galilee. He was the last of the Rephaim, a people remembered as giants, and his huge iron bed was a famous relic. Israel defeated him at Edrei just before entering Canaan, and his land went to half the tribe of Manasseh. Og and Sihon became a pair in Israel's memory, a reminder that God had already beaten the giants Israel once feared.
32314: King of Bashan, last of the Rephaim. He attacked Israel at Edrei, was defeated and killed with all his people, and his sixty cities were taken. His bedstead was nine by four cubits.
32315: The 'bed of iron' may be a basalt sarcophagus or a ritual bed. Large dolmens (stone tombs) are common in the region of Bashan.
32316: Og survived the flood by clinging to the ark and lived until Moses' day.
32317: Babylonian Talmud, Niddah 61a; Pirqe de-Rabbi Eliezer 23
32318: Huge, proud and confident in his strength and fortresses.
32324: Before Israel arrived, Sihon had captured Moabite land up to the Arnon river and made Heshbon his capital.
32326: Moses asks peacefully to pass along the King's Highway without touching fields or wells. Sihon refuses and attacks at Jahaz.
32328: Israel defeats Sihon and takes his land from the Arnon to the Jabbok.
32330: Generations later Jephthah tells the king of Ammon that Israel took this land from Sihon, not from Ammon.
32331: Sihon was the Amorite king of Heshbon, east of the Jordan. He had seized land from Moab. When Moses asked politely to pass through his territory, Sihon refused and attacked. Israel won, and his land became the home of Reuben and Gad. Deuteronomy says God 'hardened his spirit', echoing Pharaoh. Sihon's defeat, with Og's, became a key memory of God's faithfulness.
32332: Amorite king at Heshbon who had taken Moabite land. He refused Israel passage, attacked, and was defeated, and Israel took his land from the Arnon to the Jabbok.
32334: Deuteronomy 2:30 says God hardened his spirit. As with Pharaoh, interpreters debate how this fits with Sihon's own choice to refuse peace.
32335: Suspicious and aggressive, a conqueror unwilling to let another people through.
32343: Seeing what Israel did to the Amorites, Balak and Moab are terrified. 'This company shall lick up all that are round about us.'
32345: He sends rich gifts to the seer Balaam to come and curse Israel.
32347: Balak builds altars on three high places and offers sacrifices. Each time Balaam blesses Israel instead.
32349: Balak claps his hands in fury and dismisses Balaam, who pronounces a final oracle of a star coming out of Jacob.
32351: Micah calls Israel to remember Balak's scheme. Revelation says Balaam taught Balak to lead Israel into idolatry and sexual sin.
32352: Balak son of Zippor was king of Moab when Israel camped on his border. Afraid to fight them, he tried to defeat them with words, hiring the famous seer Balaam to curse them. Again and again Balaam could only bless Israel, and Balak's plan collapsed. Later Scripture remembers Balak as one who tried to turn God's people against God, first by curse and then by temptation (Numbers 25 and Revelation 2:14).
32353: King of Moab, son of Zippor. He hired Balaam to curse Israel, built altars on three high places, and was frustrated when Balaam blessed them instead. Joshua 24:9 says he 'warred against Israel'.
32354: Balak shows that no curse can overturn God's blessing (Numbers 23:8). Revelation uses him as a picture of seduction into compromise.
32355: The weekly Torah portion bearing his name (Balak) is read as a lesson that God turns curses into blessings (Deuteronomy 23:5).
32356: Anxious, impatient and commanding, a king who thinks the right price can buy any outcome.
32361: Because Israel did evil, God strengthens Eglon. Allied with Ammon and Amalek, he takes the City of Palms (Jericho) and rules Israel for eighteen years.
32363: Ehud, a left-handed Benjamite, brings tribute, then claims a secret message from God. Alone in the king's cool upper room, he stabs Eglon, a very fat man, and escapes while the servants wait outside.
32365: Ehud rallies Israel, they seize the Jordan fords, and ten thousand Moabites die. The land has rest eighty years.
32366: Eglon was a king of Moab who ruled over part of Israel for eighteen years, based at Jericho. Judges says God strengthened him because Israel had turned away. He was assassinated by the left-handed judge Ehud in one of the Bible's most vivid and darkly comic scenes, full of details about his size and his servants waiting outside the locked door.
32367: King of Moab who, with Ammon and Amalek, took Jericho and dominated Israel for eighteen years. He was very fat. Ehud killed him in his upper room and Israel then defeated Moab.
32368: The story mocks the foreign oppressor. His name sounds like 'calf', and he is described like a fattened animal ready for slaughter.
32369: Comfortable, self-indulgent and easily flattered by a promised secret.
32376: With an ox goad, a long pointed stick for driving cattle, he kills six hundred Philistines and saves Israel.
32378: Deborah's song says that in the days of Shamgar the highways were deserted and travellers used back roads, because the land was so unsafe.
